title: unique_ptr
lesson:
Unit 3 ended with a question: **who owns this object?** `std::unique_ptr` (from `<memory>`) answers it in code. A `unique_ptr` is a small RAII object that holds a pointer and **deletes the object in its destructor**. There is exactly one owner at a time.

```
#include <memory>

auto boss = std::make_unique<Enemy>("Troll", 200);   // new, but owned
boss->hp -= 50;                                      // use it like a pointer
if (boss) { ... }                                    // empty or not?
// no delete anywhere: the Troll is deleted when boss goes out of scope
```

Always make them with `std::make_unique<T>(args...)`, never `new`. One line, no way to leak.

**Exactly one owner.** You can't copy a `unique_ptr` (two owners would delete twice), so the compiler stops you:

```
auto a = std::make_unique<Pickup>("gem", 50);
auto b = a;              // error: can't copy
auto c = std::move(a);   // fine: ownership moves to c, a is now empty (nullptr)
```

`std::move` doesn't move any memory; it says "I'm handing this over". After it, the old variable is empty.

**Functions say who owns what** just by their types:

- `void add(std::unique_ptr<Pickup> p)`: the function **takes ownership**. Callers write `add(std::move(p))` or `add(std::make_unique<Pickup>(...))`.
- `std::unique_ptr<Pickup> take()`: the caller **receives ownership**.
- `void inspect(const Pickup& p)` or `Pickup* find()`: just **using** it, no ownership. A raw pointer from `.get()` is fine for looking, as long as the owner outlives your use.

**Vectors of unique_ptr** are the classic game entity list:

```
std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Entity>> entities;
entities.push_back(std::make_unique<Entity>("Goblin", 30));
for (auto& e : entities) e->hp -= 5;     // & : you can't copy them
entities.erase(entities.begin());        // that Entity is deleted right here
entities.clear();                        // all of them deleted
```

Removing from the vector deletes the object. Destroying the vector deletes them all. No destructor to write, no leaks.

**The common mistake:** keeping a raw pointer (from `.get()` or `&*e`) to an entity, then erasing it from the vector. The pointer now dangles. Decide clearly which code owns, and look things up again by name or id instead of holding pointers for a long time.

Unreal's version is `TUniquePtr<T>` with `MakeUnique<T>()` and `MoveTemp()`. Same idea, engine spelling.

notes: make_unique builds the object and wraps it in its owner in one step.
adopt takes a unique_ptr by value, so callers must hand ownership over with std::move.
After std::move(boss), boss is empty; checking it with if/? shows that.
Loop with auto& because unique_ptrs can't be copied.
erase deletes that entity on the spot, and the vector deletes the rest when main ends: no delete written anywhere.

exercises.title: Make and choose pickups
exercises.prompt:
Pickup is given. Write std::unique_ptr<Pickup> makePickup(const std::string& name, int value): a new Pickup made with std::make_unique, or nullptr if value is 0 or less.
Write std::unique_ptr<Pickup> better(std::unique_ptr<Pickup> a, std::unique_ptr<Pickup> b): it takes ownership of both and returns the one with the higher value (a on a tie). The other one is destroyed. If one of them is null, return the other.

tests.call: []{ auto p = makePickup("gem", 50); return p ? p->name : std::string("null"); }()
makePickup("junk", 0) == nullptr
[]{ int before = Pickup::alive; auto p = makePickup("gem", 50); auto q = makePickup("coin", 5); return Pickup::alive - before; }()
[]{ auto r = better(std::make_unique<Pickup>("gem", 50), std::make_unique<Pickup>("coin", 5)); return r ? r->name : std::string("null"); }()
[]{ auto r = better(std::make_unique<Pickup>("coin", 5), std::make_unique<Pickup>("gem", 50)); return r ? r->name : std::string("null"); }()
[]{ int before = Pickup::alive; auto r = better(std::make_unique<Pickup>("a", 1), std::make_unique<Pickup>("b", 2)); return Pickup::alive - before; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: The winner survives (owned by the caller); the loser is destroyed when better returns.

tests.call: []{ auto r = better(nullptr, std::make_unique<Pickup>("b", 2)); return r ? r->name : std::string("null"); }()
[]{ auto r = better(std::make_unique<Pickup>("x", 3), std::make_unique<Pickup>("y", 3)); return r ? r->name : std::string("null"); }()

hints: makePickup: if (value <= 0) return nullptr; return std::make_unique<Pickup>(name, value);
better: if (!a) return b; if (!b) return a; then compare a->value and b->value.
Returning a parameter by name moves it out automatically; the one you don't return is destroyed at the closing brace.

exercises.title: An inventory that owns its items
exercises.prompt:
Write class Inventory, which owns its items in a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Pickup>>:
- void add(std::unique_ptr<Pickup> item): takes ownership; a null item is ignored.
- int size() const and int totalValue() const.
- std::unique_ptr<Pickup> take(const std::string& name): removes the first item with that name from the inventory and gives ownership to the caller; nullptr if there is none.

tests.call: []{ Inventory inv; inv.add(std::make_unique<Pickup>("gem", 50)); auto c = std::make_unique<Pickup>("coin", 5); inv.add(std::move(c)); return inv.size(); }()
[]{ Inventory inv; inv.add(std::make_unique<Pickup>("gem", 50)); inv.add(std::make_unique<Pickup>("coin", 5)); return inv.totalValue(); }()
[]{ Inventory inv; inv.add(std::make_unique<Pickup>("gem", 50)); inv.add(std::make_unique<Pickup>("coin", 5)); auto p = inv.take("gem"); return (p ? p->value : -1) * 10 + inv.size(); }()
[]{ Inventory inv; inv.add(std::make_unique<Pickup>("gem", 50)); auto p = inv.take("ruby"); return std::to_string(p == nullptr) + std::to_string(inv.size()); }()
[]{ Inventory inv; inv.add(nullptr); return inv.size(); }()

[]{ int before = Pickup::alive; { Inventory inv; inv.add(std::make_unique<Pickup>("a", 1)); inv.add(std::make_unique<Pickup>("b", 2)); auto t = inv.take("a"); if (Pickup::alive - before != 2) return -1; } return Pickup::alive - before; }()

hints: take: loop with an index; when items[i]->name == name, auto out = std::move(items[i]); items.erase(items.begin() + i); return out;

exercises.title: A world of entities
exercises.prompt:
Write class World, which owns its entities in a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Entity>>:
- Entity* spawn(const std::string& name, int hp): creates the entity, keeps ownership, and returns a plain (non-owning) pointer to it.
- void damageAll(int amount): lowers every entity's hp by amount.
- int removeDead(): deletes every entity whose hp is 0 or less and returns how many were removed.
- int count() const, and Entity* find(const std::string& name): the first entity with that name, or nullptr.

tests.call: []{ World w; Entity* e = w.spawn("Goblin", 30); return e ? e->hp : -1; }()
[]{ World w; Entity* e = w.spawn("Orc", 20); if (!e) return -1; e->hp = 7; Entity* f = w.find("Orc"); return f ? f->hp : -1; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: spawn returns .get() of the unique_ptr the world keeps, so both point at the same Orc.

tests.call: []{ World w; w.spawn("Goblin", 30); w.spawn("Rat", 5); w.damageAll(10); int removed = w.removeDead(); return removed * 10 + w.count(); }()
[]{ int before = Entity::alive; World w; w.spawn("Rat", 5); w.spawn("Bat", 3); w.spawn("Ogre", 90); w.damageAll(5); w.removeDead(); return Entity::alive - before; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: Removing the unique_ptr from the vector is what deletes the entity.

tests.call: []{ World w; w.spawn("Rat", 5); return w.find("Dragon") == nullptr; }()
[]{ World w; w.spawn("A", 1); w.spawn("B", 1); w.spawn("C", 1); w.damageAll(1); return w.removeDead() * 10 + w.count(); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: Exactly 0 hp counts as dead, and erasing while looping by index skips items: use remove_if or only move on when you don't erase.

tests.call: World().removeDead()

hints: removeDead: loop with an index i; if entities[i]->hp <= 0, erase it and don't do i++ that time.
Or use #include <algorithm> and the erase-remove_if idiom.

quiz.q: auto a = std::make_unique<Enemy>(); auto b = a; What happens?
choices: Compile error: a unique_ptr can't be copied
quiz.why: One owner only: copying is forbidden.

quiz.q: After auto c = std::move(a); what is a?
What does void add(std::unique_ptr<Item> item) tell you?
choices: It just looks at the item
It takes ownership of the item
It deletes the item straight away
quiz.why: A unique_ptr by value means the function receives ownership.
The unique_ptr is destroyed, so it deletes what it owns.

quiz.q: You keep Entity* raw = e.get(); and later the entity is erased. Using raw now is...
quiz.why: .get() doesn't own anything; the owner deleted the entity.

cards.q: A look-only pointer from a unique_ptr?
cards.a: p.get() (doesn't own; mustn't outlive the owner)

explain: Explain what 'ownership' means for a unique_ptr, and how a vector of unique_ptrs makes a game's entity list leak-free.
